title: What is the point of cinema?

commenti.body: [removed]

I think that's kind of like saying " what's the point of art? *or" what's the point of entertainment? " or even "what's the point of information? "

I think the world without any artform be a brutal and terrible existence and with the film reel technology progressing to smartphone capabilities,  I believe the amount of high quality content is nearing what could be a silver age of independant film.

Going to the other way, artists feel a need to express themselves, tell stories, showcase techniques they like.

So I think it's a very weird headspace to not imagine the inner drive that motivates most film workers.

I mean if you're thinking critically to a negative point-
 I would say take a break from it.

Read literature or even good comic storylines, or play video games.

Just cuz you might need to emotionally recharge possibly for weeks) order to re-experience the medium doesn't mean you dislike it.  It just means that you need a rest. 

Funny enough I think I'm more concerned with the folks who don't get burnout.

I think the human need to relax and try new things something that is more normal for lack of a better word.

Cinema is art snd art is truth???  No.  At it’s best cinema is art but mostly compromise…and art as truth?  Not really.  Provocation, commerce, a mirror., flavour of the month.  What is true about cubism?  It’s just a subjective lens through which the privileged fleetingly view life.

Cinema is something you watch, and coming out of the theatre having watched it, you feel like you got something out of it: that "something" obviously isn't a tangiable thing - its more along the lines of having experienced catharsis, or elation, or whatever - but nevertheless one should feel like one got something out of it all.

That's the simplest, most straightforward and most useful way to think about it.

i think a better term for what i meant is: art is life. or art is reality. because in it's essence art is based on what we experience and what we feel, in life and in reality, it is as you said a lens through which we view life and reality.

This is like saying "what's the point of masturbating?" If you don't intuitively understand why film, cinema and movies are important, I'm not sure any argument is going to convince you otherwise. You either value movies innately or you don't. That's how I see it, at least. 

>where can we draw a line between "pure entertainment" just for the sake of it, and cinema? 

I don't think such a line exists, and I don't see any reason to try and find it if it does.

> there are films that convey no particular message, no wisdom no love, but they are still great pieces of filmmaking, so... can we consider a film with no theme or depth cinema just because it's genuinely great filmmaking?

Yes. A movie doesn't have to communicate a message, or wisdom, or love, in order to be "cinema." If it's a movie, it's cinema. 

I dunno. I guess I'm not entirely sure what you're asking?
I completely Agree!
I do understand why film is important to me, i just want to get different povs and opinions.

Every movie is cinema but not every movie is art. Some people think of cinema as strictly a form of entertainment and others think of it strictly as an art form. I find that the most tolerable people are the ones who accept it as both.

For me cinema explores ideas, concepts, characters that make me look at my life differently. It's both entertaining, highly interesting and I gain something else, new knowledge, a new perspective. 

I find all these ingredients to be something I want out of at least 20-30% of my viewing experiences. If it was all just 100% pure mindless entertainment I wouldn't value it at all. It wouldn't be anything other than a time waster.
Yes this is what i think.

I think the bigger question is why cinema, over painting, literature, dance etc, as a form of art. What can cinema offer that these don't?

I've only seen a few movies that have actually tried to deal with that question.
How does one distinguish between art and just cinema?

One complication here is that mere entertainment often acquires the status of art in hindsight: Mozart's operas, Dickens' novels (and the novel in general), jazz. 

In film, Hitchcock's reputation, with the help of *Cahiers du Cinéma*, has risen from 'crafter of commercial thrillers' to 'one of the greatest and most influential artists in film history.'

I don't like competition because I think different mediums have different pros and cons ( books allow for great movies in the imagination, video games allow for nonlinear storytelling, TV has seasons that can flesh out characters more novelistically, I think movies are great for providing immediate emotional responses)

There is no objectivity in art, only impact.

Cinema has the ability to be both things. Whether someone sees a movie as art is mostly up to the viewer themself. It’s all about what the viewer thinks and experiences. The problem now, is many peoples preconceived notions, leading to a refusal to give a film a chance to be something greater than just entertainment.

Would you say that art is important? and if yes, why do you personally think that?  

I myself do think art is important, but sometimes after so much overthinking deeply, i find myself wondering what am i doing?, asking myself, why watch a film at all? lol.

To explore their own interior life. To empathize with persons or stories one wouldn't usually witness. To feel and experience aethetic beauty. To be inspired. To remember something. To get a new outlook on life. Etc. (imo)

>The problem now, is many peoples preconceived notions, leading to a refusal to give a film a chance to be something greater than just entertainment.

I feel like that's always been the case, though.

Look at the ten highest-grossing films of any given year in the twentieth century; it will have quite a few forgotten crowd-pleasers and very little in the way of Fellini, Bergman, Malick, or any other auteur you'd like to name. 

The fact is the true cinephile with a Criterion Channel subscription and David Bordwell on their bookshelf is a tiny minority compared to the Marvel Cinematic Universe audience. 

And this certainly isn't unique to film. *Ulysses* was published just over a century ago. How many people are taking the time to read it in 2023? How many people did so in 2003, or 1983, or 1963? But a relatively small group of readers discovers it and joins the 'cult' every year. The same with Mahler's symphonies or Chardin's paintings.

Sometimes a work, even an all-time great work, is just not for everyone. 

Re: your first point, you're absolutely right. *In An Experiment in Criticism* (I don't have the book handy at the moment) C.S. Lewis writes of the need to take a book as it is, on its own terms, to let one's imagination be guided by it, to get beyond whatever preconceived notions one has about it or its subject matter. To be open minded, put simply. 

But in film, as in every other medium, genre conventions and other factors do bring certain expectations.

I would say that it's important, and I think possibly the best argument for it is the simple fact that every single culture in human history has developed some sort of visual art, music and storytelling. It clearly has a deep, universal importance for our species.

I agree with you.

Why does it have to be a competition? It's not like one has to choose between watching movies or reading books for the rest of one's life.

Yeah maybe it has always been that way. I won’t pretend to know, but I just imagine that people were more open to the films of Bergman and Fellini then, compared to the openness of general audiences to modern art house films today.

Agree, they can all co-exist, like reading and listening to music did for 100s of years.

I'm just curious about the medium of film being explore more, like the boundaries of it being pushed. I think we have a lot of film movements that are just around the corner. 

One for example is the silent films, which had to craft a whole new way of story telling.

I think this is one of those things that really doesnt quantify what the point of anything is. We exist on this planet for a limited time for literally no reason at all. It just is. We don't have a point so why should anything else?


Who is to say what is and isn't important? Nothing is, realistically. So we make our own personal judgement on what we value and what is worth our time. Art doesnt have to have a message, it doesnt have to philosophise, it doesnt have to give meaning or add knowledge. Why do you think this? Do you believe there are no paintings that are just there to look nice? Or to entertain us? And why is this less valuable? In fact why does the intent even matter when its the outcome that does. 


Who is to say that something created simply to entertain, something we have seen many times doesnt have any value? I think it does.


Theres a famous quote, often probably misattributed to john lennon, "Time enjoyed is never time wasted" for its the good times that keep life worth living. Its laughing and enjoyment that drives us forward. That is important. That is art. That is beautiful. While you might scoff at the concept of a movie like stuber, but if you watched it and managed to enjoy 2h of time on this meaningless existance? Then perfect, what more do you need

I would imagine that I think art is much more important than most people think. Art has the capacity of accomplishing so much. It can change people, it captures moments in time, it offers many perspectives on essentially everything to ever exist. Now you might ask what the point of that even is but at that point you’d just be approaching nihilism in a sense. 

In regard to you interpreting a film I would say if you find yourself overthinking and asking yourself what you’re doing, then the piece doesn’t mean enough to you, which is not a you problem. That just means that it doesn’t connect with you at this stage in your life. Then comes the most beautiful thing about cinema, you watch it 20 years later and maybe it’s the most impactful thing you’ve ever seen.

I once heard art defined as something that makes you feel something in your mind, body, and soul - thought provoking, elicits a physical reaction, elicits an emotional reaction. It’s not perfect but if I get all three, I know what I’ve seen is true art, to me at least. It’s all subjective.

Very interesting topic and lots of amazing thoughts in this thread.  

I can’t really add much to what has been said so I’ll just quote Tarkovsky

Cinema like no other art has the power to widen, enhance and concentrate a persons experience, to make it longer, significantly longer. It lets us assimilate our selves to world and others. It inspires us to be humble, compassionate, forgiving. It gives us understanding, it gives us peace. 

Ultimately Tarkovsky concluded, the allotted function of art is not, as is often assumed, to put across ideas, to propagate thoughts, to serve as example. The aim or art is to prepare a person for death. To plow a harrowing his soul, rendering it capable of turning g to good. 

Thoughts?

It's not that complicated

Humans like to make stuff

Some paint, some sing, some make movies with a camera.

Some consider something art, some don't

As long as it's sustainable it might be produced, if it's being enjoyed there might be more of it

The only justification for any sort of production is if the person who produced it thought it was viable for him

It's a free market, it's inherently neutral and not positivistic or utilitarian.

It's just whatever

As the other commenter said, different mediums work differently and help us see differently. 

Right now, movies and television are uniquely positioned as the dominant art form in culture. They have the best opportunity to get a message into the hands of as many people as possible. People don’t read as much, they don’t listen to albums as much, and they haven’t been taking art or dance seriously for decades.

In our current climate, that’s their primary advantage. Maybe video games have some of that opportunity as well, but IMO there are way fewer video games that work as art than movies. I say this as someone who’s been playing video games since I was a kid - I love them, but they rarely accomplish something as profound as changing the way I think, which movies do all the time.
Yes exactly, when a piece connects with you, it doesn't require thinking or logic, that connection and it's importance can be felt, and through that feeling everything makes sense.

And now with advanced 3D film technology, the medium can be pushed and explored like never before, we are yet to see what can we do with the new capacities that we have today. 

But would that ever be done? "true filmmaking" or "cinema" if there is such a thing is now boxed into this little category called indie films, with little budget and interest gravitating toward it.

And now with advanced 3D film technology, the medium can be pushed and explored like never before, we are yet to see what can we do with the new capacities that we have today. 

But would that ever be done? "true filmmaking" or "cinema" if there is such a thing is now boxed into this little category called indie films, with little budget and interest gravitating toward it.

Yes i completely agree with you, video games are mostly produced for entertainment only, you rarely see games that carry depth or meaning.

One game that comes to my mind and that has had such and impactful effect on me, is "Life is strange", it was a very beautiful experience that helped me through a rough period in my life. Its probably the most meaningful and artistic game i have ever played, yet not as enjoyable as red dead redemption 2 lol.
I don't think i got you, could you please further explain?

I agree, i also think that art in general is extremely important, because of how it provides meaning, in our world meaning can be found in different philosophies and ideologies, but ultimately something we can agree on is that what really matters is things like love, friendship and beauty, and art is essential because it helps us with understanding those things and sharing them.

I don't think that art needs a message or a philosophy, we are mostly on the same side, i don't think enjoyment is worthless, **im merely trying to acquire different thoughts and ideas**. I do think that movies can be made and watched just to have a good time, there is absolutely nothing wrong with that, and no one has the right to tell anyone that "what you're doing is wrong, and that is not art", or "that is not cinema", because art and cinema are fluid notions. Art is obviously subjective and different things matter to different people. 

With that being said, i do personally value films with depth, and most of what i consume is art that resonates with me and that teaches me about life.

We are apparently on a meaningless ride, but that simply isn't enough for us, "we are a tragic misstep in evolution", "we are creatures that should not exist by natural law", and yet we do, and we wonder and look for answers and purpose, but if we can't find it objectively, we can at least find it subjectively, we can enjoy beauty, nature and connection, so if life is meaningless, our experiences and emotions are what gives it meaning, this is what i look for in art, this is what i need, film to me is extremely important, and i don't always watch 2h just to have a good time, film  has the capacity to help us understand what really matters for us, what we want out of this ride, or maybe how can we sustain a healthy relationship, or perhaps it can teach us how to deal with a rough period, the point is, art can be simply beautiful and enjoyable, but it has the capacity to be even more, it can be meaningful, helpful and informal, and in that sense film as an art form, functions at it's best.

Well it obviously means different things for different people, but that is great as long as they get something from it, we can at least agree that there are films that serve as art and function in the sense that Tarkovsky means, or the sense that Scorsese means, and there are films that function simply as an enjoyable experience, that is not wrong, but it's a different thing meant for different people.
yes! i would have included in my ect. lol.

In your original post, you write about drawing a dividing line between cinema which is true art and cinema which is mere entertainment. 

I think it's important to note that, throughout history, works have crossed that dividing line -- risen, in retrospective perception, from the status of popular entertainment to the status of art. If that is the case, and it seems to be, then we really need to consider how subjective our perceptions of which films (or books, or whatever) truly act as "a lens through which we view life and reality" are. And how that perception can change over time. New generations can discover a work and see depths in it that weren't apparent to its original audience.

In short, it's hard to divide art from just entertainment.

Consider 1957, which saw the release of *The Seventh Seal* and *Nights of Cabiria*. The highest grossing films in the US were:

1	The Bridge on the River Kwai	Columbia	$15,000,000\[1\]  
2	Peyton Place	20th Century Fox	$11,000,000\[1\]  
3	Sayonara	Warner Bros.	$10,500,000\[1\]  
4	Search for Paradise	Cinerama Releasing	$6,500,000\[1\]  
5	Old Yeller	Buena Vista	$5,900,000\[1\]  
6	Raintree County	MGM	$5,830,000\[2\]  
7	Island in the Sun  
A Farewell to Arms	20th Century Fox	$5,000,000\[3\]  
8	Pal Joey	Columbia	$4,700,000\[3\]  
9	Gunfight at the O.K. Corral	Paramount	$4,300,000\[3\]  
10	Don't Go Near the Water	MGM	$4,265,000\[2\]

How many of these movies, with the exception of *Kwai*, are remembered as classics or at all discussed in the context of greatness or of film history?

The arthouse audience has always been a small minority of moviegoers.
